entries.title: OpenAI Is About to Release Its First AI Model With ‘Critical’ Cyber Abilities
entries.summary: The company will give select partners early access to its Astra AI model—so they have time to shore up their defenses.
entries.content:
OpenAI announced Tuesday that its forthcoming AI model, Astra, is its first to reach the company’s threshold for what it calls “critical” cyber capabilities. OpenAI says it plans to publicly release a version of Astra “soon,” but will make the model’s advanced cyber capabilities available only to select partners in its Daybreak Blue early-access program at launch.

In a briefing with reporters, OpenAI safety and security leaders said the company has concluded that Astra reaches the critical cybersecurity capabilities outlined in its preparedness framework, which sets thresholds and protocols for when its AI models pose new levels of risk. The company says an AI model has reached its critical cyber threshold when it can independently find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world software. OpenAI leaders said the company has followed its procedure for this situation, which is to halt further development until appropriate safeguards and security measures can be implemented.

OpenAI previously said that it paused some training workloads related to the development of Astra and a future AI model for several weeks. Executives say the company has now resumed said work on Astra, and the future AI model, after putting additional safety and security controls in place. OpenAI says the multi-week pause was productive, and it is now confident that it can release Astra broadly in a safe way.

The announcement comes as Silicon Valley grapples with the advanced cybersecurity capabilities of cutting-edge AI models, and tries to assure users, lawmakers, and other companies that it can keep them under control. In July, OpenAI disclosed an incident in which agents running two of its models exploited vulnerabilities in what was supposed to be a siloed testing environment, gaining access to the internet and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face. (OpenAI notes that Astra was not one of the models involved in this case.)

Other AI companies, such as Anthropic and Meta, have disclosed similar incidents in recent weeks. On Monday, Anthropic also said it has paused some AI training workloads while it hardens its safety and security practices.

OpenAI says it’s implementing a multi-step approach to limit everyday users from accessing Astra’s advanced cyber capabilities, including a new “misalignment monitor.” If someone asks Astra to help them find an exploit in a real-world software system, for example, the model is supposed to refuse to answer. OpenAI says it has also made Astra more robust to jailbreaking attempts, and in tests it successfully refused unsafe queries at a significantly higher rate than previous models.

However, OpenAI notes in a blog post that its misalignment monitor may “occasionally flag legitimate activity as potential cyber misuse or unauthorized behavior, leading to it inadvertently being slowed, paused, or stopped.” OpenAI says the guardrail can be triggered in some cases even when a user is engaging in activities that don’t appear related to cybersecurity. When this happens, ChatGPT and Codex users may be asked to review the model’s action before proceeding, OpenAI said.

Partners in OpenAI’s Daybreak program—which includes digital infrastructure providers like Cisco, Cloudflare, and Palo Alto Networks—will get early access to a less restricted version of Astra with more robust cyber capabilities. The goal of the program is to ensure these companies can use advanced AI models like Astra to harden their defenses before similarly capable models are made broadly available. OpenAI leaders also said the company has been working closely with government partners to ensure they’re aware of Astra’s cyber skills and can get access to them.

Astra is not only capable of finding novel software vulnerabilities and developing ways to exploit them for hacking, but is also able to “chain” multiple exploits together, a technique used to bore deeper and deeper into a target system and gain access that wouldn’t be attainable using just one vulnerability.

According to figures from OpenAI, Astra outperforms industry leading AI models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic’s Mythos on cybersecurity benchmarks such as ExploitBench, which Astra scored 100 percent on. However, these capabilities are broadly in line with the rising hacking abilities of AI models that OpenAI and Anthropic have been forecasting for months. In April, for example, Anthropic emphasized that Mythos Preview was able to autonomously develop exploit chains.

As the AI and cybersecurity industries have scrambled to adapt, though, many cybersecurity experts have emphasized that key digital security defenses and longstanding best practices are still durable. However, AI puts organizations and systems that haven’t fully implemented these protections at even more urgent risk.

entries.title: The Diamond Moon and Other Astronomical Events To See in September 2026
entries.summary: September is full of opportunities to expand your knowledge of the night sky. Mark your calendars.
entries.content:
August set the bar high for stargazers, with two eclipses and the peak of the Perseids meteor shower. But it’s not time to put away your telescopes, with some lesser-known astronomical events set to arrive across the sky this month.

The Pleiades will appear next to the moon, Venus will reach its brightest point of the year, Neptune will be in its best position for spotting with a telescope, and as an encore to the Perseids, there will also be a smaller meteor shower.

Here are some dates worth marking on your calendar for the month to come.

Venus near Spica: September 1 and 2

September begins with an easy opportunity to spot two of the brightest objects in the night sky. Venus will appear near Spica, the most intense star in the constellation Virgo. Both objects will be visible to the naked eye.

The exact timing of Venus’ appearance is September 2 at 00:17 UTC. This means that, depending on the your location, the conjunction could occur in the afternoon or evening of September 1.

It should be easy to tell the two celestial objects apart. Venus will shine much more brightly, looking like a white dot that doesn’t twinkle as much as the stars. Spica will appear nearby as a considerably fainter bluish dot. The two will be approximately 1.5 degrees apart.

A handy trick is that 0.5 degrees in the sky is roughly the average diameter of a full moon. Therefore, once you find the brightest point in the sky—which will be Venus—you can find Spica about three moons away.

A Diamond Studded Moon: September 3

The moon will be accompanied by one of the most famous star clusters in the sky. On the night of September 3, it will appear approximately 1.1 degrees from the Pleiades—close enough to observe both objects in the same region. The moon will be about 59% illuminated, according to Star Walk’s calculations.

The Pleiades, also known as “the Seven Sisters” or M45, is a star cluster located in the constellation Taurus. Six or seven of its members are usually visible to the naked eye under good conditions, although the cluster contains hundreds of young stars. These stars were born at approximately the same time and remain gravitationally bound together.

The proximity to the waning moon offers a good opportunity for spotting them. To the naked eye, they will appear as a small group of bright points next to the moon, as if they were diamonds. Binoculars will allow you to make out many more. The encounter will happen again on September 30, when the two objects will once more be separated by just one degree.

A Modest Meteor Shower: September 9 and 10

September also has its own meteor shower. The Epsilon Perseids will peak between September 9 and 10, producing up to eight meteors per hour.

The number of meteors is lower than that of the famous Perseids in August. However, this shower has one advantage: its peak will occur just two days before the new moon, making the sky ideally dark for viewing.

Conditions will be especially favorable from the northern hemisphere, and, as with any meteor shower, it is recommended to find a dark location away from light pollution.

Venus at Its Brightest: September 22

Venus is usually one of the easiest objects to spot in the night sky, but toward the end of September it will shine even brighter. The planet will reach an apparent magnitude of approximately -4.8. By comparison, the full moon has a magnitude of -12.7, and Sirius—considered the brightest star in the sky—barely reaches -1.46.

Look for the planet after sunset, near the western horizon. Viewing conditions will be best from the southern hemisphere.

The Equinox: September 23

Unlike the other events on this list, the equinox isn’t something we can go out and observe directly. Instead, it’s an astronomical moment that marks a specific point in Earth’s orbit and, with it, the change of season.

The September equinox will occur on September 23 when the Sun crosses the equator as it moves southward. The event marks the astronomical beginning of fall in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere.

Neptune Is in the Neighborhood: September 26

Spotting Neptune is considerably challenging compared to other planets. The most distant planet in the solar system (sorry Pluto) is forecasted to reach opposition on September 26. This means that Earth will be approximately between Neptune and the Sun.

This positioning means Neptune will remain visible for much of the night and will be at one of its closest distances to our planet for the year. Therefore, September offers one of the best opportunities in 2026 to try to spot it.

It’s too faint to be seen with the naked eye. You’ll need a telescope and to know its position among the stars of Pisces. Even then, it will appear as a tiny bluish disk.

Harvest Moon: September 26

September will end with a particularly famous full moon. The full moon closest to the September equinox is traditionally called the Harvest Moon. The term does not describe a distinct physical phenomenon, nor does it mean that the moon will change color, size, or brightness. It’s a traditional name related to the harvests of the northern hemisphere.

entries.title: Best Amazon Labor Day Deals (2026): Sony, Shark, Anker
entries.summary: These are the 15 best Amazon Labor Day deals on WIRED-tested, WIRED-recommended products in 2026.
entries.content:
Amazon doesn't advertise its Labor Day sale as heavily as Prime Day and Black Friday, but the Amazon 2026 Labor Day Sale still offers some of the best deals of the year on an assortment of tech and home gear ranging from half off WIRED's previous top-pick wireless headphones, Sony's XM5 series ($198) we've ever tested to the best deal I've seen this year on WIRED's favorite laptop power bank, the EcoFlow Rapid Pro X ($180).

Amazon's deals are in heavy flux during the lead-up to Labor Day—and a number of my favorite grills and griddles have already sold out on Amazon days before the actual holiday. You can find the latest trending and lightning deals at Amazon's Labor Day Sale page here. But in the meantime, these are the best dozen or so Amazon Labor Day deals right now.

Also see WIRED's best early Labor Day deals on tech gadgets, mattresses, tool sets, kitchen devices, and REI deals.

Best Amazon Labor Day Deals 2026

WIRED’s Previous Top-Pick Wireless Headphones for $198 ($200 Off)

Sony's XM5 wireless headphones immediately became WIRED's favorite wireless headphones when they came out in 2022—a top-dog position they gave up only to last year's next-generation noise-canceling phones from Sony, the WH-1000XM6. The previous-model XM5's remain truly excellent headphones: light and comfortable, with great control, great noise canceling, and accomplished sound in pretty much every regard. They're also on sale for the lowest price we've ever seen them, during Amazon's Labor Day Sale.

$60 Off WIRED’s Current Top-Pick Headphones

This said, if you simply must have the best wireless headphones on earth, that's still the next-gen XM6, which also rank as the best noise-canceling headphones on earth, with exemplary sound, 30 hours of battery life, and seven times the processing power of the XM5s. They're on sale for $60 off MSRP during the Labor Day Sale. It's a sale we've seen before multiple times this past year, but still nearly the lowest price we've seen.

Nothing Ear (3a) Earbuds for $79 ($20 Off)

The Nothing Ear (3a) earbuds are a stylish answer to noise-canceling earbuds. Nothing's buds consistently among WIRED's honorable mentions for their excellent value and bold design. The newest offer call recording and audio transcriptions, and ease of pairing with iPhones and Android devices. The active noise cancellation is hardly the best in the game, but at $79 you won't easily find better: This is the lowest price we've seen since these earbuds dropped this summer.

A Top-Line Sonos Soundbar for $899 ($200 Off)

WIRED's reviewer called the Sonos Arc Ultra a marvel of sound engineering when it arrived this year, a full update of the original Arc and an unmitigated triumph for Sonos: big bass, excellent clarity, and especially immersive Dolby Atmos sound. Sonos has also mostly cleared up the problems with its app in this update, thank god. This matches the best deal we've seen on it this year on Sonos' newest flagship soundbar.

The Newest Amazon Echo Spot for $70 ($40 Off)

The Amazon Echo Spot is a bit of a twofer. It takes some of the best smart-display features—like a clock and weather readouts—and pairs it with a decent-enough smart speaker, while leaving out the, uh, corporate video surveillance. No one needs a camera in their bedroom! Anyway, this is a pretty decent discount.

Apple AirTag (2nd Gen) for $25 ($5 off)

Never buy an AirTag at full price. The newest-gen AirTags remain the best Bluetooth tracker for anyone committed to Apple, and you'll somehow always have need of more. But luckily they always go on sale during Amazon sales events. This Labor Day deal matches the Prime day price this year, and is the best price in 2026 so far.

The Best Laptop Power Bank for $180 ($100 Off)

This is the best laptop power bank that WIRED reviewer Simon Hill has tested, barely edging out Anker's devices for its unusually rapid charging capability. With 300W fast-charging, this EcoFlow comes pretty close to the maximum allowed laptop power bank. For Labor Day, it's on sale for the cheapest we've ever seen it.

A Power Bank With a Charging Dock for $180 ($50 Off)

But if you prize convenience, this Anker offers the same storage capacity as the EcoFlow, but with a handy charging dock. This Anker Prime Power doesn't charge quite as fast as the EcoFlow, but it comes pretty close. This is the lowest price this Anker has been in a few months.

Cuisinart Air Fryer Toaster Oven TOA-70NAS for $158 ($72 Off)

Whenever this Cuisinart toaster oven and air fryer dips below $200, it's one of the best deals out there. It crisps wings preternaturally well for an oven model—perhaps better than any oven-shaped air fryer I've tested. It browns evenly and keeps steady and accurate temperature. This said, it's a much more analog experience than most modern air fryers. This keeps it durable, but flashy it ain't.

My Favorite Meat Probe for $153 ($47 Off)

A wireless meat thermometer has become a wild necessity in these times of salmonella … or just if you like well-cooked meat. Two birds, amirite? Anyway, after trying a half-dozen meat thermometers this past summer alone, this Typhur Sync Gold is my favorite overall for its mix of excellent signal and the easy-to-read, display on its compact base station—meaning it's useful both for outdoor and indoor use. This Sync Gold set goes on sale here and there, and this Labor Day price matches the lowest price I've seen this year.

Aeocky Rhea-001 Dehumidifier for $230 ($70 Off)

This dehumidifier from Aeocky has gotten unusually good reports back on durability, a claim I'm busy testing since receiving the device this summer. My only complaint was that I thought I could do a little better for the price. A steep price cut for Labor Day pretty much alleviates this complaint, just in time for mold season.

A Great Sous-Vide Cooker for $169 ($60 Off)

Sous-vide can seem intimidating. But WIRED reviewer Kat Merck recommends this touchscreen Anova immersion circulator for its gentle learning curve: You just clip it onto a pot of water, select your temp, and let it go. Sous-vide is, of course, a terrific way to slow-cook meat to the appropriate temp. But in these troubled times, you can also home-pasteurize your eggs to make sure they're free of salmonella. This Labor Day discount isn't the lowest price I've seen, but it's certainly one of the better deals I've seen since the prices all went up this year.

The Best Robot Vacuum at (Nearly) Its Best Price: Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal for $750 ($650 Off)

This is the best robot vacuum WIRED tested, at quite nearly the best price we've seen it during Amazon's 2026 Labor Day sale. If you don't feel like rolling the dice and waiting for Black Friday, the Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal is a terrific robot vacuum with UV light that shows you perhaps too much about previous spills, and built-in AI that smartly takes care of even difficult messes. The extendable arm is also a bonus, reaching areas other vacuums can't.

WIRED’s Favorite Handheld Pet Vacuum for $70 ($20 Off)

This handheld pet vacuum from Shark goes on sale reasonably often, but this is still the best deal so far this season on WIRED's favorite handheld pet-hair remover. The UltraCyclone Pro is lightweight, powerful, and designed to stop pet hair from tangling up the vacuum's brush—with a wealth of attachments for funny surfaces and crevices. WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell also attests it can do double-duty as a Cheerio-picker-upper, when toddlers are about.

The Best Outdoor Lights for $350 ($90 Off)

It's nearing the time of early darkness. A set of permanent outdoor lights can keep this from becoming dreary at home, and this set from Govee is WIRED's favorite smart lighting setup for everyday illumination and Christmas lights both. This deal crops up reasonably often, but it's the best you're likely to find till the end of the year.

entries.title: Sonos Ace Ultra, Beam Ultra, Sonos Fabric, and a New App: Everything Sonos Just Announced
entries.summary: Sonos is cramming AI into its software because it’s “very hot these days.” The new features, which include agentic automation, are opt-in.
entries.content:
Sonos has a new app. Stop me if you’ve heard this one before.

The smart speaker company, long a darling of the audio industry, undid much of the goodwill it earned with its multiroom speakers through a bevy of software updates that broke its app in 2024. Almost all app users hated it, citing the loss of features like volume control and accessibility tools meant to help blind people use the wireless speaker system. Sonos eventually owned up to the mistake, considered bringing back the old app again, then booted its CEO and marched its new leaders out to apologize profusely to win back the company’s furious customers.

Now, Sonos says it has a brand-new app update, infused with lots of generative AI features. The company also announced a new soundbar and its second pair of over-the-ear headphones. Sonos representatives say it doesn’t want to be seen as a speaker company anymore, but as something bigger and more holistic.

“For years people have been seeing us as a speaker company,” says Brandon Holley, the interim hardware lead at Sonos. “What we actually are is an audio operating system.”

The company is calling that operating system Sonos 27, and it manifests in a few ways. First and foremost: updates to the Sonos app.

Sonos 27 App

Sonos knows that the words “new Sonos app” might strike fear in the hearts of its users.

“When I say that out loud, I know exactly what comes to mind,” Sid Patel, vice president of software at Sonos, tells WIRED. Patel says the app was developed with a “customer-centric feedback listening approach” that involves reaching out to the community and being active in forums like Reddit. New features to make the app easier to use will include improved tab navigation, better room sorting, and changes to volume knobs on the app itself. In the fall, Sonos will release system health views that let you diagnose connection issues for each product.

The big feature is Sonos 27voice, the company’s generative AI integration, which is being released in early access. It lets you talk to the speakers like you would Amazon’s Alexa or a Google Home speaker, allowing you to request music based on your mood. It also has a Model Context Protocol, which can connect to your AI service of choice if you want to ask ChatGPT to play music on your speakers.

The company is highlighting its Sonos Custom Agents, which let users customize their agents to do various tasks throughout the system, like triggering speakers in a certain room at a certain time. You can also change the voices used if maybe you’d like the AI in your kitchen to sound like a fancy French chef, or have your bathroom speaker talk to you like a pirate.

“Obviously AI is something that's very hot these days, clearly,” Patel says. “So we have integrated various pieces of AI into our system.”

When asked what products Sonos 27 and its AI features would work with, a Sonos representative wrote via email that Sonos 27 will work in Sonos’ S2 app, but not the S1 app—the version that controls some older Sonos equipment. So owners of older Sonos hardware won't be able to access these new AI features.

“Sonos 27 is designed to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities, so not every product will support every new feature,” the representative wrote. “We want to be transparent about those limitations while continuing to support products with security and ongoing updates for as long as the hardware allows.”

Despite the stated effort to be transparent, Sonos says it won’t release details about compatibility or upgrade paths for each product until “a later date.”

Sonos Fabric

Sonos has an official name for the network its products use to sync across rooms: Sonos Fabric.

“Sonos Fabric is the name of the magic that has existed for what Sonos was built on,” Patel says. “The idea of, you have one speaker, two speakers, three speakers, and how they magically work together in a home theater setup or a bonded setup or group.”

Two new features are coming to that newly christened technology. One is what Sonos calls portable surround, which enables users to take devices from one room to another and have them sync there. So if you have a main soundbar by your TV but want to bring in another couple of speakers from other rooms to act as surround sound speakers for movie night, the Sonos products can detect their location and moderate which audio to play where.

Second is the ability to switch audio between the speakers and headphones, which Sonos calls Headphone Linking.

Sonos Ace Ultra

Sonos’ first pair of over-ear headphones arrived in 2024, right during the height of the Sonos app woes. The Sonos Ace were very good, except the headphones didn’t work within Sonos’ speaker ecosystem. Sonos wants to fix that problem with its follow-up headset, the Sonos Ace Ultra.

It has 35 hours of battery life and can connect to devices via USB-C and 3.5 mm. More importantly, it can connect to other Sonos speakers via Wi-Fi. The Ace Ultra runs on Sonos Fabric, which means it can connect to your wider Sonos system and let you switch playback between speakers and the headphones

“With a single push of a button, you'll be able to suck music into your headphones,” Patel says.

Sonos Beam Ultra

Sonos introduced a new soundbar, called the Beam Ultra. It’s an upgrade of the company’s existing Sonos Beam with nine drivers, four more than the past Beams. They’re also upward-firing drivers that bounce the sound off your ceiling for better acoustics. The Beam Ultra has AI-enabled features, like AI speech enhancement that aims to make dialog more discernible in loud scenes. The Beam Ultra can connect via Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and wired HDMI eARC.

This is a lot of change for Sonos, something the company hasn’t always handled gracefully. Sonos’ home systems already aren’t the easiest to set up, sometimes requiring separate apps for older products. The company may be rejiggering itself as an “audio operating system,” but its software has long been the source of its troubles with getting its products to work right. Will AI smarts fix that? Maybe for its newer devices. But anyone with an existing system may still struggle.

The AI features on products and in the Sonos 27 app will be opt-in, meaning you can avoid them entirely. “That really is our new approach to our app release,” Patel says. “We're going to bring our customers along. We're going to listen more.”

That would be a good plan. Sounds like Sonos’ speakers will be listening more, too.

entries.title: Using High-Energy Laser, US Shoots Down Drones Near Mexico Border
entries.summary: The US Army’s laser system is part of a new generation of directed-energy weapons capable of detecting, tracking, and destroying drones with a concentrated beam of light.
entries.content:
This week, the US Army used a high-energy multipurpose laser to shoot down three drones near the US-Mexico border, which official reports claimed were “posing a physical threat to US military personnel and CBP partners,” referring to Customs and Border Patrol.

The operation took place between the night of August 25 and the early morning of August 26 in the vicinity of the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and was led by the Joint Task Force Southern Border (JTF-SB), which operates under US Northern Command. Authorities confirmed that, during the operation, agents used technology derived from the Army’s High-Energy Multipurpose Laser (AMP-HEL) system, a military program focused on implementing high-energy lasers for new defense capabilities.

Available information suggests that this initiative began in September 2025, when AeroVironment, a company specializing in defense technology, delivered the first two functional prototypes of these laser-based weapons to the US Armed Forces. Two new, improved systems were delivered as the program was expanded in December of the same year. According to the manufacturer, this particular platform, called the Locust Laser Weapon System, is designed to be mounted on military vehicles, as the Army has done with the versions its received.

Operating at 20 kilowatts, the Locust system relies on an extremely concentrated beam of light that, in various phases, allows for the detection, tracking, illumination, damaging, or destruction of targets at a distance. Locust and other high-energy laser (HEL) systems typically use sensors, cameras, radars, or other means to locate an object. Once identified, the system focuses the light beam on the target with great precision, even when it is moving. It then uses an additional electrical energy charge to increase the beam’s power and convert it into heat. This ultimately damages or disables the drone, the exact outcomes depending on factors such as distance, exposure time, and the target’s characteristics.

In addition, Locust’s most recent versions—such as the one delivered to the military last December—include radar and command-and-control systems. These make it easier to integrate the weapon into a more complex mobile defense platform, rather than using it as a stand-alone device.

The exact location of the operation remains unknown. Nor is there any concrete information regarding the origin of the neutralized drones or the entities responsible for their operation. However, Curtis Taylor, commander of JTF-SB, suggested that the aircraft could be linked to criminal cells involved in drug trafficking and operations in Mexican territory.

“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners. By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance. We also greatly appreciate the support of our Mexican Army partners as we work together to combat this threat to the border region,” the major general stated in a press release.

The official statement also does not specify the exact models from the AMP-HEL program that were used in the operation. However, the international press has linked the action to the campaign against illegal immigration and drug cartels that President Donald Trump has been waging since he began his second term.

During his election campaign, Trump promised to combat both issues by implementing drastic measures, especially along the US-Mexico border. To that end, his administration has deployed a wide variety of technologies, HEL systems being just part of the growing toolkit.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: 5 Best Folding Phones (2026): Samsung, Google, Motorola
entries.summary: Ready to move on from the traditional glass slab? Introduce a hinge into your life with these folding smartphones.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

You may be scoffing as you read this. The best folding phones? Really? Aren’t those just gimmicks? I'm here to tell you they're pretty darn useful. And yes, there are quite a few now, so you have options. Folding phones are an evolution of the traditional single-screen slab of glass we've all been using for nearly two decades—and we might even see a folding iPhone in 2026.

They largely come in two forms: a folding flip phone or a folding book-like phone, enabling you to either relive the glory days of small phones or expand your multitasking options while on the go. A folding phone is a personal decision—arguably even more than a traditional smartphone, since it hinges (heh) on what style you prefer. We have tested almost all of them, and these are our favorites.

Check out our other mobile buying guides, including the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Best Google Pixel Phones, Best Motorola Phones, Best Phones With a Headphone Jack, and Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US.

Updated August 2026: We've added the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Motorola Razr Ultra (2026), Motorola Razr (2026), Honor Magic V6; mentions of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Flip8, Motorola Razr Fold, Motorola Razr+ (2026), and Oppo Find N6; removed some older devices; and updated prices.

Other Folding Phones to Consider

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: The Z Fold8 Ultra is a refined release with a 6.5-inch cover display that opens to an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side. It's fast and smooth, with a 5,000-mAh battery, but it's the camera that earns it the “Ultra” title. It's an impressive combo, including a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Sadly, it lacks Qi2 support for magnetic wireless charging, and the camera module makes it rock when lying flat on a surface. But the main reason it misses out on a place above is that the smaller Fold8 is so much easier to handle.

Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 for $1,200: We haven't had a chance to spend much time with the Flip8 yet, but based on what we have seen, it's a close second to Motorola's Razr Ultra. It is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world with a redesigned chassis. It has a 4.1-inch cover screen, and it flips open to become a 6.9-inch candy bar. It's also more durable than ever and boasts the same excellent chipset and performance as Samsung's larger Fold models. The 4,300-mAh battery is solid, but the camera system is relatively basic, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide.

Motorola Razr Fold for $1,900: The first book-style foldable from Motorola is good, but not great. The front screen feels very much like a normal phone, and you can open it to enjoy the vast 8.1-inch display inside. Sadly, the Razr Fold lacks the top-end processor of the year, which is disappointing at this price. The highlight is the massive 6,000-mAh battery, which can stretch to nearly three days of use. Thankfully, it does come with seven years of software updates (unlike Motorola's Flip family). Motorola has also added a telephoto lens to the capable camera, though it can't compete with Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Motorola Razr+ 2026 for $1,100: The awkward middle child in the Razr lineup lacks the bells and whistles or top-notch specs of the Ultra, but still costs more than $1,000. You can get very close to the same experience from the cheaper Razr and save hundreds. Even battery life is unimpressive, because it has the smallest capacity of the Razr family. The cover glass isn’t the ceramic glass mixture as on the Razr Ultra. I found out the hard way after dropping the phone once, roughly a 4-foot drop onto asphalt, and the front screen shattered. Get a screen protector!

Oppo Find N6 for $1,929: With an 8.12-inch internal display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its promise of being creaseless, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it when the screen is on, though you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide. The global model can use familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import it, as this phone won’t officially be released in the West.

Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold for $1,799: The only reason to consider the Pixel 10 Pro Fold right now is if you see it on sale. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is superior, but the 10 Pro Fold isn't far behind this year's release. It's still a reasonably slim device with a large front screen that feels like a normal phone, an excellent 8-inch inner screen, and a triple-camera system that delivers great results, though not as great as the Pixel 10 Pro series. Read our Best Pixel Phones guide for more.

Xiaomi Mix Flip for $899: Xiaomi’s first flip phone has a lovely design with excellent displays inside and out, long battery life with fast charging, and flagship-level performance, which makes a nice change, as flip phones often have middling specs. It also boasts a solid dual-lens camera, opting for telephoto instead of ultrawide alongside the capable main shooter, which is more useful for most folks. The software lets the party down a little; there’s no IP rating, and it is pricey, but I had fun with this flip phone.

Things to Know Before Buying

Folding phones are more fragile than normal phones. Folding phones have more parts than a traditional smartphone, not to mention a hinge. Companies advertise how many folds these devices have been tested for—usually around 200,000 or 500,000 folds—but a single drop can be incredibly damaging. They are not as dust-resistant, and some aren't as water-resistant (only the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is IP68-rated in the US), so you'll want to be especially careful. Use a case, and it may be worth investing in the manufacturer's device care policy.

Don't remove the built-in screen protector. Most of these folding phones have a film over the inner screen. You might be tempted to remove it, but don't—it can damage the display. The packaging usually includes instructions not to remove it and how to care for your device.

There's a small learning curve to the software. Flip-style folding phones are fairly straightforward, but book-like folding phones that double as tablets have new multitasking tricks that will take some getting used to if you want to make the most of them. I recommend taking some time to run through these features so you understand how they work.

They're expensive. Do you need one? Nobody needs a folding phone. If you think you'll benefit from one, know they're frequently discounted during big sale events like Black Friday, and you can also knock a few hundred dollars off if you trade in an eligible device.

Which Type of Folding Phone Is for You?

Folding flip phones are for people who want a compact device. Think of a normal phone you can fold in half. That's pretty much what you get, plus a screen on the front to monitor widgets and texts. This does mean you can flip the phone to answer a call and flip it shut to end one—super cool. You can put the phone at a 90-degree angle, and some apps will adapt to show controls on the bottom and important details at the top, like in video calling apps or when watching videos on YouTube, though this depends on the phone. Folding flip phones typically have mediocre battery life, and their cameras aren't as good as their non-folding counterparts.

Folding book-like phones are for people who want the big-screen experience. Are you constantly watching full-length movies on your phone? Or do you always find yourself jumping back and forth between two apps? Then these are for you. They have good battery life and better cameras (though not as good as non-folding phones), but they're far more expensive. These include the short-lived triple-screen folding devices like Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold. They're thick and heavy, though we're seeing newer models that are surprisingly thin. Still, you may have a hard time fitting them in your pockets.

Is Now a Good Time to Buy?

If you're team Android, this is a good time to buy. Samsung and Google just updated their foldables, and Motorola released its first big foldable in the summer and won't announce the Razr 2027 lineup until the spring. For folks outside the US, we probably won't see new foldables from Honor or Oppo until the spring, too.

If you're considering an iPhone, Apple is likely to unveil a new folding phone soon, so you might want to wait and see what it looks like.

My Favorite Folding Features

Whichever style you go for, my favorite feature of folding phones is the ability to see the viewfinder on the external screen and snap a selfie with the high-quality rear cameras—just set the phone down slightly folded so it stays upright, and there's usually a button you can click in the camera app to send the preview to the external screen. You can usually trigger the shutter hands-free with a palm gesture. (Motorola's Razr Ultra lets you start and stop video recordings with hand gestures, too!) It's excellent when traveling if you want to take a photo of yourself next to a point of interest.

Many of these phones offer similar functionality with translation—Samsung and Google, for example, let you show your words translated on the external screen so the person you are speaking to can see it, and then they can tap a button on the screen to have the phone start translating their words, which you'll see on the internal screen. It's a much nicer system than using Google Translate on a candy bar phone.

entries.title: Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless Headphones Review (2026)
entries.summary: The flagship headphones get up to 57 hours of battery life and have easily replaceable batteries.
entries.content:
Audio that’s easy to enjoy. Huge battery life with ANC on. User-replaceable battery is an important step. Comprehensive codec support. USB-C and 3.5-mm wired listening for hi-res audio. All-day comfort.

TIRED

ANC won’t win awards. Bass-forward tuning might not suit you. Build quality feels a bit more plastic than premium. Not a vast upgrade of the Momentum 4. Feel slightly overpriced.

We’ve waited almost four years for a new pair of Sennheiser Momentum wireless over-ear headphones. That’s eons in a world where Sony, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins have been busy launching stellar Bluetooth headphones like the Sony WH-1000XM6, Apple AirPods Max 2, and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3.

Plenty has happened in the intervening years—not least, Sennheiser’s consumer division being sold to hearing aid company Sonova, which is currently looking to sell it on. Thankfully, the Momentum 5 is a hugely enjoyable pair of premium headphones with some unexpectedly good features, and not the product of a troubled homelife.

Battery Life for Life

The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless look good. They strike a middle ground between premium cans (AirPods Max 2, Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3) and more lightweight ones (Bose QuietComfort Headphones, Sony WH-1000XM5). The 10.3-ounce build is mainly plastic, and the ear cups are basic, but the denim trim on the top of the comfortable headband adds fun texture. They are not head turners like the Nothing Headphone (1), but they are still nice to look at, and come in blue denim (pictured), black, and white.

They are, however, very comfortable, with a great level of squish to the earpads. Massive ears (like mine) have room to flap, and the headband doesn’t add any uncomfortable pressure. No over-ear headphone is perfect to wear with glasses, but I happily wore these for hours. When temperatures hit 95 degrees Fahrenheit my ears got sweaty, but so did the rest of me, to be fair.

The Momentum 5 Wireless get up to 57 hours of battery with ANC on, according to Sennheiser. That’s almost double what the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 can do. It’s three hours shy of the older Momentum 4, and 13 hours less than the similarly priced Marshall Monitor III ANC.

I didn’t perform an exact test on the 57-hour battery claim, but it seems fairly accurate in my real-world use thus far. I have been using the Momentum 5 daily for the past month, and they are still at about 50 percent charge.

The more interesting story to me is that the battery can be easily replaced. Remove the left ear pad, unscrew four Phillips-head screws, lift the cover, and the battery can be unplugged and swapped out in seconds.

iFixit has been showing us how to replace batteries in electronics for years, but this is the first time I’ve seen a headphone brand actively encourage consumers to do it themselves. I think Sennheiser embracing our right to repair is worth celebrating, even if, at the time of publication, the replaceable battery isn't available for purchase.

Lively and Warm Sound

The Momentum 5 Wireless supports SBC, AAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX Lossless, and aptX Adaptive codecs, plus multipoint connectivity. Plug in using either the 3.5-millimeter jack or the USB-C port to get digital lossless audio (up to 24-bit/96 kHz).

The Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app is where you can customize ANC levels, transparency, an eight-band EQ, connection preferences, and Dolby Atmos. You can also save sound profiles based on your location, maxing out ANC when you hit the office, for instance.

Controls on the headphones themselves are touch controls on the right ear cup, and they work fine: as in, they didn’t annoy me. A tap pauses music, swipes adjust volume and skip tracks, while a double tap toggles between ANC and transparency modes.

Active Noise Cancellation comes via eight microphones, and it is good, verging on great. It works well on public transport, provides a cocoon in cafés, and gifts solitude in a shared office. If you’ve never used Sony or Bose ANC headphones, you’ll be delighted with the Momentum 5s, but if you’re switching from those two brands, you might find these a bit of a letdown. We’re talking small margins here, but the Momentum 5 just lacks that eerily quiet sealed-off feeling of the WH-1000XM6 or Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen).

Call quality is good too, and the wind-reducing mics kept my voice front and center, but it’s not the reason I’d buy these headphones.

I tested the Momentum 5 Wireless using the best and worst playback resolutions from Spotify—both over Wi-Fi and cellular. I also listened to Qobuz hi-resolution recordings and my own digital music library. And no matter what I played, the headphones offered me a smooth, refined, and expressive performance.

They’re not “high-fidelity” in the sense that the extreme edges of a recording are not exposed, and they happily make poor-quality output sound enjoyable. That said, you’ll get a bit more out of them by listening to higher-fidelity sources. And if you’re still playing the lowest-resolution audio playback on Spotify (or don’t even know what I am talking about), you don’t need to spend $399 on a pair of headphones.

Mixing it up between the pop of Olivia Rodrigo’s excellent new album, the twang of Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band, via Wu-Tang, and more of the Police than I’m comfortable admitting, the Sennheiser made every genre enjoyable to listen to and were totally agreeable. They’re not neutral, with plenty of relaxed warmth to the sound profile.

Listening to the Sennheisers side by side with the B&W Px7 S3, I noticed a little lack in punch and drive by comparison. The opposite is true when listening to them against the AirPods Max 2, however, with the Sennheiser’s classy midrange cutting through the mix with real authority. This was also the case when comparing them with the now discontinued Momentum 3 Wireless from 2019 (although I wish Sennheiser would bring back the sumptuous leather earpads at least as an add-on).

They are bass-forward, though, and anyone leaning toward acoustic or classical would do well to tweak the EQ via the app. The sound is clean overall, with a tight thump, although not a patch on the taut rumble from the more expensive AirPods Max.

Should You Buy Them?

The Momentum 5 Wireless are long overdue, but at $399, they face stiff competition from more mainstream competitors like Sony, Bose, Apple, and Bowers & Wilkins, all of whom have launched serious good over-ear headphones recently. This hasn’t left a lot of room for Sennheiser to compete in, but, sensibly, the brand hasn’t tried to win every battle.

The ANC is very good (but not spookily quiet), and the design is classy (but not indulgent). Sound is warm, expressive, and easy to enjoy for long periods of time, even if the bass might need taming in the EQ. But importantly, Sennheiser has created a headphone with superb battery life, easy wired and hi-res listening, an impressive codec list, and an easily replaceable battery you can swap yourself.

They are not the most exciting headphones in any one area, but they are comfortable, considered, likable, and impressively repairable.

entries.title: 3 Best Sleep Tracker Picks for Optimizing Your Sleep (2026)
entries.summary: I tested the top sleep wearables for every type of sleeper, including devices from Oura, Google Fitbit, and Eight Sleep.
entries.content:
One of the most notable shifts in sleep technology is the transition from passive tracking to active guidance. Increasingly, consumer sleep trackers are offering AI-driven coaching and personalized recommendations that help users translate data into healthier habits. When thoughtfully implemented, this evolution has meaningful potential to improve outcomes.

But at the same time, there's a valid concern that as sleep tech becomes more advanced, it may also become more prescriptive. The key is to ensure that these tools remain supportive rather than directive, encouraging better sleep quality without fostering pressure, perfectionism, or unnecessary anxiety.

To find the best trackers for most people, I've spoken with experts and tested a ton of wearables, from smart rings and smartwatches to headbands and non-wearable devices. After years of snooze monitoring, these are the favorites.

For more health and wellness tracking, check out our guides to the Best Smart Rings, the Best Smartwatches, and the Best Fitness Trackers.

Featured in This Guide

Updated September 2026: I've added the Google Fitbit Air and the Oura Ring 5, along with information about Oura's recent class-action lawsuit. I've added the Google Pixel Watch 5 to Honorable Mentions; prices and links were also updated.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

How I Test Sleep Trackers

Sleep trackers can't diagnose a sleep disorder or replace a clinical sleep study, but the best ones offer reliable data and actionable insights and are comfortable enough to use overnight. Here's how I test them:

  • I wear each device continuously for at least a month to reveal meaningful trends. Long-term testing also helps evaluate consistency, comfort, and whether the companion app remains useful after the novelty wears off.
  • I test trackers during normal life rather than in controlled conditions. That includes irregular bedtimes, travel days, and the occasional insomnia spiral.
  • I compare sleep data across multiple devices I'm testing simultaneously, paying close attention to metrics including: total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep stages (light, deep, REM), resting heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), respiratory rate, and blood oxygen levels (SpO2).
  • I evaluate comfort for overnight wear. I test devices across different sleeping positions to judge whether they feel bulky, restrictive, or irritating during slumber.
  • I test battery life and charging speed against manufacturer claims.
  • The software experience is just as important as the hardware. I evaluate how clearly each companion app presents information, whether the insights feel personalized, and whether a subscription is required to unlock key features.
  • Depending on what's available on each device, I also evaluate smart alarms, sleep coaching recommendations, and integrations with broader health ecosystems like Apple Health and Google Health.
  • I monitor reliability and long-term performance by checking for syncing issues, app crashes, and inaccurate sleep recordings.
  • Some sleep trackers lock advanced sleep analysis behind monthly memberships. I consider whether the premium features justify the ongoing costs.

What Am I Testing Next?

I am testing the new Ultrahuman Ring Pro and the RingConn Gen 3. I'm also reevaluating the Whoop MG, the Muse S Athena Headband, and the Withings ScanWatch 2.

Best Sleep Tracker Overall

Of all the fitness trackers I’ve tested, the Oura Ring’s sleep assessment has been one of the most accurate. The ring has a multisensor suite: an 18-path multi-wavelength photoplethysmography (PPG) to monitor blood oxygen levels (SpO2), heart rate, HRV, and respiratory rate; a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor to track body temperature; and a 3D accelerometer that captures movement, including your sleep stages and nighttime restlessness. It tracks factors like total sleep, time in bed, and sleep efficiency on a nightly basis via a time graph and displays trends on a weekly or monthly basis. Auto-detected naps are also factored into your sleep score, which is a huge bonus. The Oura has been the most comfortable to wear to bed, plus the app is user-friendly. You can view your sleep score, as well as personalized tips on optimizing your bedtime.

Note: You do need Oura’s $6-per-month membership to unlock the more advanced health metrics. Without it, you can only view your sleep, readiness, and activity scores and access recorded meditations. But the subscription is worth it and relatively affordable compared to its competitors.

Is There a Class-Action Lawsuit Against Oura?

In August, San Francisco’s Clarkson Law Firm filed a class-action lawsuit alleging that Oura rings cannot measure one’s sleep or cycles and rely on the company’s AI models to do the guesswork. The complaint argues that Oura overstates the accuracy of its sleep tracking, pointing out that sleep is “defined by brain electrical activity, eye movements, muscle tone, and other signals measured through electrodes placed on the scalp, leads on the eyes, and sensors on the chin. [Oura] doesn’t measure any of these parameters.”

In an email statement to WIRED responding to the lawsuit, an Oura spokesperson wrote, “Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature.”

According to Oura, its sleep-staging algorithm is informed by research based on more than 1,200 nights of collected data. “We published a peer-reviewed paper that describes how the sleep-staging algorithm was developed and how it uses the signals collected by the ring,” wrote the spokesperson. “Multiple third-party, independent studies support our claims of accuracy, and we have transparently reported on the mechanisms and measures that inform Oura’s sleep staging.”

I’ll continue to monitor the lawsuit and report back on any significant developments. For now, though, nothing has surfaced that changes my judgment of Oura as my top pick.

Best Screenless Band

If you prefer a wristband, the Google Fitbit Air is a screenless tracker that's super comfortable to wear to sleep. According to Google, the Air is 15 percent more accurate than its predecessor, with better sleep-stage detection, improved nap tracking, and a new restlessness bar. I particularly appreciate how this sleep tracker handles gaps in data. One night, my Air slipped off, so the next morning the app gave me a poor sleep score based on three hours of recorded data. After I manually corrected the sleep window, the Air didn’t retroactively generate a new score or fill in the missing metrics with its proprietary algorithm. It acknowledged that it didn’t have enough information, which, in a market of AI-generated guesses, I found refreshing.

The app presents your data in a super digestible way; it doesn’t drown you in graphs, charts, or wellness jargon. Its AI Health Coach also sends morning check-ins with sleep recaps, saving you from having to interpret the data yourself. You can also prompt the coach to turn those insights into actionable recommendations. Most of the sleep insights are locked behind the Google Health Premium subscription, which costs $10 per month. It’s a reasonable price compared to its competitors, especially since Google gives you a three-month free trial when buying any new Fitbit device.

Best Contactless Sleep Tracker

The Eight Sleep Pod 5 is, by far, the best alternative to a wearable I've discovered. It's a mattress cover that not only tracks your sleep but also regulates your temperature. It cools to 55 degrees Fahrenheit and warms to 110 degrees Fahrenheit, with real-time adjustments based on your sleep metrics. If you sleep with your partner, you can set different temperatures on each side of the bed, and it will track each of your sleep patterns independently. The Pod 5 also introduces physical temperature buttons, so you can manually adjust based on personal preference.

When it comes to sleep tracking, the Pod 5 delivers many of the same metrics you'd get from a wearable, including sleep scores, total sleep time, sleep stage breakdowns, HRV, and respiratory rate. Eight Sleep also sends a daily morning text that distills your data into a quick summary, so you don't even need to open the app to see how you slept. There were some discrepancies in the data, especially in the sleep score, compared to the Oura Ring 4, which I consider my gold standard for accuracy, but it's reliable enough if you want to avoid wearables. Plus, if I forget to wear my Oura to bed, I have my Eight Sleep auto-tracking my slumber in the background.

Eight Sleep requires a 12-month commitment to its Autopilot plan. The subscription includes automatic temperature adjustments, sleep reports, software updates, and a vibration and thermal alarm. After 12 months, you can still use the Eight Sleep without the subscription via its manual controls, but you wouldn't have access to sleep reports, which defeats the point.

Honorable Mentions

Google Pixel Watch 5 for $400: The Pixel Watch 5 is my favorite Wear OS smartwatch for Android, thanks to its elegant design, excellent accuracy, and compact size. You do need to pay for a Google Health Premium subscription ($10 per month) to see deeper sleep insights, including but not limited to your long-term sleep trends, changes in your sleep patterns, and resting heart rate. It does a fair job of tracking naps, and with any kind of sleep, you'll be able to see your sleep stages and your blood oxygen saturation.

Google Pixel Watch 4 for $350: With the launch of the Pixel Watch 5, I wouldn’t recommend buying its predecessor at full price. But if you find it on sale, I’d snag it; the Watch 4 will still get the same software updates as Google’s latest and greatest.

Whoop MG for $239 (Peak): A screenless tracker that's more comfortable to sleep with than an Apple Watch but more expensive than the Google Fitbit Air. Along with your sleep performance score, it tracks metrics like sleep sufficiency, consistency, and efficiency. In testing, the sleep coach was pretty comprehensive, offering personalized bedtime and wake-up recommendations based on your strain levels. You can toggle on a haptic motor that will wake you with a little wrist-based buzz, although given that the Whoop is screenless, you'll need to double-tap the center of your device or reach for your phone to disable the alarm from the app. Former reviewer Adrienne So also found Whoop to be a little frustrating because it would recommend more sleep than she was capable of getting.

Apple Watch Series 11 for $399: If you already have an Apple Watch Series 4 or later, you can use it to track your sleep. Between the heart rate sensor and the accelerometer, your Apple Watch can break your slumber down into four stages. Newer models can also measure blood oxygen and temperature. It feels like a general overview compared to some of the other sleep trackers I tried, but it does offer a sleep score, which Apple debuted last fall. —Adrienne So

Garmin Epix Pro (Gen 2) for $1,100: All of Garmin’s fitness trackers track sleep to some extent, but the Epix Pro has what Garmin calls advanced sleep monitoring, or the ability to track sleep stages, your blood oxygen saturation, your respiratory rate, and restlessness. Contributor Adrienne So found that the Epix Pro regularly accounted for her getting a half-hour to an hour more sleep than she actually got most nights, as double-checked by a Whoop and Oura. It also doesn’t add naps to your sleep score.

Google Nest Hub (2nd Gen) for $100: The Nest Hub uses radar to track your sleep, which means you don't need to wear a tracker; it also has a microphone to track snoring, sleep talking, and other nocturnal sounds. I love the Nest Hub on my nightstand for smart-home controls, family photos, and listening to sleep sounds or podcasts in bed, but the sleep tracking consistently overestimated my REM phases and missed periods of wakefulness that other trackers recorded. When I used multiple trackers simultaneously, the Nest Hub was the outlier. —Simon Hill

Muse S Athena Headband for $475: This headband has sensors capable of tracking your brain activity, similar to an electroencephalogram (EEG), alongside an accelerometer and gyroscope, and a PPG sensor to measure heart rate and blood circulation. It’s chiefly a meditation aid designed to help you relax, but it can also track your sleep by recording your heart rate, respiration, time to fall asleep, and how much you moved around for an overall sleep score. Sadly, I found it uncomfortable to wear and often woke to discover the sleep tracking had failed, usually because I’d removed it during the night. —Simon Hill

Withings Sleep Tracking Mat for $200: Another alternative to wearables, this sensor-packed mat from Withings slips underneath your mattress where your chest rests. You need to calibrate it during the initial setup, but it’s quick and easy. It tracks your movements, breathing, and heart rate throughout the night, detects snoring or other sounds, and alerts you about potential breathing problems that might indicate sleep apnea. I have doubts about the accuracy, as it assumes you are trying to sleep if you are lying still in bed watching TV or reading, and that can skew your score (though it’s best to only use your bed for sleep if you suffer from insomnia). I found it often marked periods of wakefulness as light sleep. It requires a power outlet, but that does mean you never need to worry about charging. —Simon Hill

Withings ScanWatch 2 for $370: Wear the Withings ScanWatch 2 to bed and you will get a sleep score out of 100 in the morning. It covers the same four stages as other trackers (awake, REM, light, and deep) but boasts a PPG sensor for measuring your respiratory rate. It can also track your heart rate, temperature, and blood oxygen levels. The ScanWatch 2 provides a wealth of data and advice in the Withings app. Some folks may find it bulky and uncomfortable for sleep, though, and it had problems distinguishing between light sleep and when I was lying awake in bed. —Simon Hill

Sleep Routine: Tracker & Alarm for $60/year (iOS/Android): Sleep Routine is a sleep-tracking app that provides a report for each night, breaking your sleep into stages. Reviewer Simon Hill says the results were somewhat accurate and broadly matched the Ultrahuman Ring Air, but the app can be a bit wonky. There were frequent occasions where he'd get an error message the morning after with no report or a brief recorded sleep. There was also no indication of why it failed. You can test Sleep Routine for a week before you need to subscribe.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Wearables More Reliable Than Contactless Trackers?

Most consumer sleep trackers, whether wearable or contactless, typically analyze movement, heart rate, and respiration to infer how you sleep. In general, these devices do a decent job at measuring sleep duration and overall trends, but accuracy can vary widely from one tracker to another.

“Wearables often capture heart-rate-based signals more consistently, while contactless devices avoid issues like discomfort or forgetting to wear them,” writes sleep scientist and clinician Joseph Dzierzewski in an email. “Neither category matches the precision of clinical sleep studies, especially for sleep staging.”

TL;DR: Both types of sleep trackers are useful for identifying patterns over time, but neither delivers medical-grade accuracy.

What Sleep Metrics Should You Pay Attention To?

According to sleep experts, total sleep time remains the most dependable metric that consumer sleep trackers can provide. “It's not perfect, but it tends to be the most stable and actionable,” writes Dzierzewski in an email.

Sleep stage tracking is far less precise. “They're inferring brain states from indirect signals, so misclassification is common,” writes Dzierzewski. While those insights can still be useful for spotting long-term trends, experts caution against reading too much into nightly fluctuations.

Many sleep trackers also condense your data into a single sleep score. While these scores can offer a quick snapshot, the underlying algorithms are often proprietary and lack transparency. “For most people, focusing on consistent sleep timing, total sleep duration, and how rested they feel during the day is far more meaningful than chasing a score,” writes Dzierzewski.

Should You Use a Sleep Tracker?

It’s important to note that there’s no one-size-fits-all set of rules for better sleep. You must listen to your own body, but try not to obsess over it. That said, sleep tracking can be useful. WIRED checked in with the sleep experts for some advice:

  • Sleep trackers can increase awareness of sleep and encourage healthy sleep behavior. Establishing a bedtime routine is crucial if you want to improve your sleep quality. Nitun Verma, spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, says sleep trackers can help people go to bed—and get out of bed—at optimal times. Dzierzewski says these devices can reveal how your sleep changes between weekdays and weekends, how alcohol or late-night meals affect recovery, and how important consistent routines are to your sleep. That kind of visibility can be incredibly motivating, considering self-monitoring is one of the most effective ways to improve health behaviors.
  • But sleep tracking can also become counterproductive. “If checking your sleep data is creating stress, or if your sleep has actually worsened since you started tracking, that's a strong sign to step back,” says Dzierzewski. “Putting the device away for a week or two can help reset your perspective. Sleep works best when it's guided by internal cues, not dictated by a number on a screen.”
  • Sleep trackers can help you track trends, but they can also be inaccurate. Verma suggests using data to identify changes in trends. For example, if your sleep time changed abruptly two weeks ago, you can look for changes in stress, environment, or daytime habits that might have sparked that change. You may discover disturbances that affect your sleep, and you can mitigate them in the future if they recur. He also notes that some trackers may give the impression that they're able to diagnose a medical condition when they don't have the data (or FDA approval) to back up those claims.
  • Sleep trackers must fit into your life. Think about how a prospective tracker might fit into your digital ecosystem, how easy it is for you to use, and how comfortable it is to wear during sleep.
  • Sleep trackers can help you experiment. If you want to optimize your sleep, Verma suggests using your sleep tracker to find what works for you. For example, you might try a new nighttime routine for two weeks and see if the sleep data improves. If it does, it can increase motivation to keep the habit. (It's helpful to think of sleep experiments in weeks rather than days to give changes a chance.)

Meet the Experts

  • Joseph Dzierzewski, PhD, is the senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation based in Arlington, Virginia.
  • Nitun Verma, MD, MBA, is a spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine based in California.
